title: The Varna Verse
hookLine: one verse names four groups from one body. it has been used to rank people by birth, and fought over ever since
carry: one body, and careful hands for a hard verse
tomorrow: where did the moon come from?
last: A WORLD THAT COMES FROM GIVING.

lines: WHAT WAS HIS MOUTH? HIS ARMS?
AN ANSWER THAT'S BEEN FOUGHT OVER.
cards: When they divided the Purusha, into how many parts did they arrange him? What was his mouth? What were his arms?
What are his thighs and feet called? That's the Purusha Sukta's eleventh verse, in paraphrase, nothing but questions, like a teacher quizzing a class. The answer comes in the next verse.
It's short, and it has been recited, defended and fought over. You met the caste question on day ninety-five, and in the Gita on day two hundred twenty-two. Today, the verse itself.

teach.b: Verse twelve answers, in paraphrase: the brahmin, the priest, was his mouth. His arms were made the rajanya, the ruler and warrior. His thighs became the vaishya, the people of trade and farming.
From his feet the shudra, the laborer, was born. Four groups, from one body. Notice the wording.

teach.h: ONE BODY. THE WORD VARNA ISN'T THERE.
teach.b: The verse doesn't use the word varna, the later word for these social orders, and it doesn't say higher or lower. But readers have heard a ranking in mouth and feet, and that's where the argument begins.
Some traditional readers take the verse as the sacred origin of the four varnas.

teach.h: A LADDER BY BIRTH, AND ITS CRITICS.
teach.b: Over time it was also used to defend a ladder fixed by birth, and people outside the four orders altogether were treated as untouchable. Reformers, among them B. R.
Ambedkar, attacked that use of the verse directly and fought the system it was used to defend.

Other readers, Hindu teachers among them, stress that all four come from one body, and point to the Bhagavad Gita, where Krishna says the four orders were made according to qualities and actions, arguing birth was never meant to decide them.
These readings don't agree, and this path won't pretend they do. India's constitution abolished untouchability in 1950, and many Hindus today reject any ranking by birth.
If a friend asks you about caste, you can say what the text says, what people did with it, and who was hurt. A verse can be held sacred and still need careful hands.

how: Hindus read the Purusha Sukta's verse on the four groups in sharply different ways: some as the origin of the varnas, others as a picture of one interdependent body, and reformers have challenged its use to justify caste by birth.

o: a law code that lists the duties of every caste
a hymn praising the priests above all others
the hymn of one cosmic person, and the world from him

games.q: the twelfth verse — tap the pairs.

s: the verse itself uses the word varna
it names the four groups as parts of one body; varna is the later word for these orders.
the verse before it is a string of questions
when they divided the Purusha, what was his mouth? what were his arms? what are his thighs and feet called?
all Hindu readers agree on what the verse means
some read it as the origin of the varnas, some as one interdependent body, and reformers attacked its use to defend caste by birth.

games.q: the hymn asks: when they divided the Purusha, what was his mouth? what does the next verse answer?
games.why: verse twelve: the brahmin was his mouth, the rajanya his arms, the vaishya his thighs, and from his feet the shudra was born. what that means has been argued over hard.

practice: Give each part of the body the same few breaths: the mouth, lips and tongue resting; the arms and hands; the thighs, their weight on the chair; and the feet, which carry everything and are usually noticed least.
No part gets more; if you pray, you can pray for anyone who has been treated as less.

wordCard.voice: The Purusha Sukta. In its twelfth verse, mouth, arms, thighs and feet become four groups of people, and readers have argued over what that means ever since.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the later word for the four social orders; it does not appear in Rig Veda 10.90.12 itself.

sources.ref: Rig Veda 10.90.11 (when they divided the Purusha, into how many parts did they arrange him? what was his mouth, his arms, his thighs and feet?)
Rig Veda 10.90.12 (the brahmin was his mouth, the rajanya was made his arms, his thighs the vaishya, from his feet the shudra was born)
Bhagavad Gita 4.13 (the four orders were created by me according to the division of qualities and actions)
